why: Removing letters only from the ends leaves a substring, so you want the shortest substring that starts with s[0] and ends with s[-1]. One left-to-right pass remembering the latest index of s[0] gives the shortest such substring ending at each occurrence of s[-1]; the answer is n minus that length.
hints: After any sequence of front/back removals, what is left of s?
You need the shortest substring s[i..j] with s[i] == s[0] and s[j] == s[-1]. For a fixed end j, the best start is the latest i <= j with s[i] == s[0].
Scan j from left to right, update last = j when s[j] == s[0], and when s[j] == s[-1] try length j - last + 1. Answer = n - minimum length. O(n).
pitfalls: If s[0] == s[-1], a single character already has the right type ("a" has type "aa"), so the answer is n - 1.
Update the latest start before checking the end at the same index, so the length-1 case is found.
The empty string has type "", so you can never remove all letters.
constraints:
• 2 ≤ |s| ≤ 2 * 10^5
  • s consists of lowercase English letters only
